input.prompt:
You are independently reviewing a completed fix in the Callisto Rust workspace at /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch: main, uncommitted changes in the working tree — do NOT commit, just review).

## Context

This is backlog task #18 of a 31-item remediation backlog: "Reuse TagIndex's tag list in create_tags instead of re-querying git." `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/tag.rs`'s `create_tags_with_options` (called once per `callisto tag` invocation with a `PublishPlan` containing one `ReleaseEntry` per package being released) used to check whether each release's tag already existed by calling `git.list_tags(Some(tag_str))?.is_empty()` INSIDE the per-release loop — one full `git tag --list` shell round-trip (or gix operation) per release. Meanwhile `TagIndex` (available via `ws.tags()`, built once and cached in a `OnceCell` on `Workspace`) had already fetched the exact same full, unfiltered tag list during its own construction, for a completely different purpose (resolving each package's last-tag). So a plan with N releases cost 1 (TagIndex::build's fetch) + N (per-release re-queries) tag-list operations, when 1 would do.

## The fix

1. `crates/callisto-graph/src/tags.rs`: added a new private field `all_tags: std::collections::BTreeSet<String>` to `TagIndex`, populated once in `TagIndex::build` from the same `fetch_all_tags(git)?` call that already existed (no new I/O — this was already being fetched, just previously discarded after the per-package template-matching loop). Added a new accessor `pub fn contains_tag(&self, tag_name: &str) -> bool` doing an exact-string lookup against that set. Updated `TagIndex::empty()` to include the new field.
2. `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/tag.rs`: changed `let already_existed = !git.list_tags(Some(tag_str))?.is_empty();` to `let already_existed = ws.tags()?.contains_tag(tag_str);`. Also changed the function's own `GitAccess` acquisition from `let git = GitAccess::discover(&ws.root, ws.runner);` to `let git = ws.git_access();` (routing through the `Workspace`-level shared instance added in a prior task, #16, rather than a second independent discovery) — removed the now-unused `GitAccess` import (kept `GitDataSource` since `git.create_tag`/`git.create_floating_major` still need it... actually verify this yourself, don't trust my claim).
3. Added a new regression test in `crates/callisto-graph/tests/tags_tests.rs`: `test_create_tags_checks_existence_against_cached_tag_index_not_per_release`, using a 2-release `PublishPlan` and a `CommandRunner` double that counts invocations matching `args == ["tag", "--list"]`, asserting the count is exactly 1 (not 3, which is what the old code would have produced: 1 from `TagIndex::build` + 2 per-release).

## What's already verified by the implementer (me) before you look

- I mutation-tested the new regression test by hand: temporarily reverted `commands/tag.rs`'s `already_existed` line back to `!ws.git_access().list_tags(Some(tag_str))?.is_empty()` (the old per-release pattern, but still calling through `ws.git_access()` rather than a fresh discover, to isolate just the existence-check regression), reran the new test, confirmed it failed with `left: 3, right: 1` (the exact expected old-code count), then restored the real fix and confirmed byte-identical restoration via `diff`.
- `cargo build -p callisto-graph --lib --tests` — clean
- `cargo test -p callisto-graph` (full crate) — all 240 lib tests pass, all integration tests pass (`tags_tests.rs` now has 4 tests, up from 3)
- `cargo clippy -p callisto-graph --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt -p callisto-graph` — applied

Do NOT re-run the full suite/clippy/fmt yourself unless you have specific reason to doubt something — trust that baseline, but DO spot-check by reading code and running narrowly-scoped commands (e.g. `cargo test -p callisto-graph --lib tags::` or `cargo test -p callisto-graph --test tags_tests`) if something looks off.

## What to review

1. **Read the actual current diff** (`git diff crates/callisto-graph/src/tags.rs crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/tag.rs crates/callisto-graph/tests/tags_tests.rs`) — don't just trust this description.
2. **Semantic equivalence of `contains_tag` vs the old `list_tags(Some(tag_str))`.** The old code passed `tag_str` (an exact tag name, e.g. `"my-pkg@1.2.3"`) as a *glob pattern* to `list_tags`, relying on the fact that a literal string with no glob metacharacters compiles to an exact-match glob. Verify this equivalence holds by reading `callisto-vcs`'s `list_tags`/glob-compilation code directly — is there ANY tag name shape (e.g. one containing literal glob metacharacters like `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`) where the old glob-based check and the new exact-string-set check could disagree? This matters because `TagName`/tag templates are user-configurable via `callisto.toml`'s `tag_template` field.
3. **`TagIndex::all_tags`'s scope**: does it correctly capture ALL tags in the repo, or could it silently miss tags added between `TagIndex::build` and when `create_tags_with_options` checks existence (a staleness window)? Compare against the *old* code's staleness characteristics (which re-queried live git each time) — is the new code strictly worse, equivalent, or better on this axis? Note whether this same staleness question already applies to `TagIndex`'s pre-existing `last_tag`/`template` lookups (used elsewhere), which would mean this isn't a new risk introduced by this task.
4. **The `ws.git_access()` / `GitAccess` import change**: confirm `GitAccess` really is unused now in `tag.rs`, and that `GitDatatSource`'s trait import is genuinely still required (check what trait methods are actually invoked via `git.` in the file).
5. **New test quality**: read `test_create_tags_checks_existence_against_cached_tag_index_not_per_release` directly. Does the assertion (`tag_list_calls == 1`) genuinely prove what it claims, or could it pass vacuously under some other bug (e.g., if `create_tags_with_options` silently skipped processing releases entirely, would the count still come out to 1)? Check that `report.created_tags.len() == 2` (asserted in the test) is enough to rule that out, or if not, say so.
6. **Sibling gaps**: any other place in `callisto-graph` (or callisto-cli) that independently calls `.list_tags(...)` for an existence check that could similarly consult a cached `TagIndex` instead? Search broadly, not just `tag.rs`.

Report back concisely: a list of concrete findings (file:line, what's wrong, why it matters), separating "must fix before commit" from "worth noting but not blocking." If you find nothing wrong, say so plainly — don't manufacture findings. Keep your report under 500 words plus the findings list.

Field atlas · polyglot release engineering

Callisto

v0.3.3 · 10 crates · unsafe_code = forbid

Named for Jupiter's most heavily cratered moon — every impact still visible, layered, in order. Which is exactly what a versioning tool has to do for a codebase.

10
crates
47.8k
lines of Rust
794
test cases
14
CLI commands

Plates

  1. The coordination gap
  2. Prior art & positioning
  3. Origin of the name
  4. Layered architecture
  5. How a release moves
  6. Feature specimens
  7. Design principles
  8. Command surface
  9. Scale & rigor

Plate I

The coordination gap

Every mature polyglot monorepo hits the same wall eventually: Rust crates, npm packages, and increasingly napi-bridged packages between them — and no single existing tool understands version coordination across all three cleanly.

Callisto's specific wedge is the napi pattern: one Rust crate compiles down to N platform-specific npm packages (@pkg/darwin-arm64, @pkg/linux-x64-gnu, and so on) plus a "main" npm package that depends on all of them via optionalDependencies — and every one of those packages has to move in lockstep, in one version, across two entirely different registries. Nothing in the current tooling landscape handles that natively.

So it discovers the workspace's package graph across Cargo, npm, and PyPI; resolves version bumps from changesets across the dependency DAG; and applies them — manifests, changelogs, lockfiles, tags, publishes — without touching a file it can't roll back.

Callisto is not "the polyglot release tool." That space has real, mature, well-resourced incumbents. Callisto's defensible niche is narrower and specific: Moon workspaces, where the team prefers the changesets file format over Conventional Commits, and needs napi-style cross-registry coordination that nothing else handles. This is a real niche — but it is a niche, not a mass-market claim. docs/00-design.md §3.2

Plate II

Prior art & positioning

Callisto brings together the best ideas from @changesets/cli, Google's release-please, and nx release — and names its debts explicitly rather than pretending to invent the category.

vs. @changesets/cli

JS-only. Polyglot teams patch around it today with proxy package.json files and hand-written sync scripts — a documented, real pattern, not a hypothetical. Re-serializes JSON with destructive default formatting.

vs. release-please

Relies on fragile regular expressions for manifest edits and focuses on single-repo releases. Genuinely polyglot in scope, but has no concept of napi platform-package coordination.

vs. Nx Release

Deeply, structurally coupled to Nx's JavaScript project graph — not something you adopt independently of the rest of Nx.

vs. knope

Handles Cargo + npm dual-published packages, and its "one version across manifests" model is the direct ancestor of Callisto's own — but it writes exact versions everywhere (no npm range preservation) and has no napi awareness.

Across a nine-axis comparison in the design doc — intent-capture format, workspace support, cross-ecosystem cascade, dual-published packages, napi coordination, library-shipping, Moon-extension support, range preservation, self-publishing — Callisto is the only one of the five with native napi platform-package coordination.

The design doc also names its own risk: the changesets project has an open issue requesting native polyglot support. If that ships, this differentiation narrows. Stated plainly, in the doc's own words — not hedged out of a pitch deck.

Plate III

Origin of the name

Jupiter's moon Callisto is the most heavily-cratered body in the solar system — and that's the point.

Every impact over roughly four billion years is still visible, layered, in order — which is what a versioning tool preserves for a codebase. docs/00-design.md §1, "Naming"

At the time of writing the name was unclaimed on crates.io; the bare name on npm belongs to an unrelated, abandoned framework, so the project publishes there scoped as @orin-dx/callisto.

Plate IV

Layered architecture

Ten crates in four strata — each layer depends only downward, the same one-directional rule that makes a crater record legible.

Fig. 1 — crate dependency layers (license split noted per crate)

■ Permissive — MIT OR Apache-2.0

■ AGPL-3.0-only

Everything else — the coordination logic, the CLI, and the Moon plugin. Preserves dual-licensing optionality; the load-bearing argument for the crate boundary itself is the layering, not the license.

Plate V

How a release moves through the system

Every command is a pure function returning a plan, plus a separate step that touches disk — modeled explicitly on release-please's compute/apply split.

Fig. 2 — changeset to published package

    SCC --> CASCADE["cascade bumps
topo order, per-edge-kind"]
    CASCADE --> APPLY["apply
CST edit + atomic write"]
    APPLY --> CHLOG["changelog + tag"]
    CHLOG --> PUB["publish
cargo / npm / twine"]

    classDef step fill:#F7F5EF,stroke:#CFC9B8,color:#211D16
    class CS,GRAPH,SCC,CASCADE,APPLY,CHLOG,PUB step
    linkStyle default stroke:#8B8570,stroke-width:1.5px

The cascade step is where the real decisions happen: for each dependency edge — Runtime, Dev, Peer, Optional, Build — it checks whether the dependent's existing semver range already covers the new version, and only escalates a bump when it doesn't. A Peer edge that falls outside its declared range can be configured to escalate all the way to a major bump.

Plate VI

Feature specimens

Eight systems, each solving one specific failure mode observed in existing tools.

CST-preserving editsmanifests
Every manifest write goes through toml_edit's concrete syntax tree or a JSON indentation-fingerprinting pass — never regex, never destructive re-serialization. Comments, key order, and whitespace survive every bump.
Atomic, crash-safe writespersistence
Temp file in the same directory → fsync → atomic rename → fsync the parent and grandparent directories. A killed process never leaves a half-written manifest. Gated by a capability token, not a code-review reminder.
Topological cascade enginegraph
A petgraph DAG runs Tarjan's SCC before any bump math — circular dependencies get caught before they ship, not discovered in production.
Version groupsfixed / linked
Fixed groups lock-step to the max computed bump; linked groups share severity but keep independent offsets. A napi crate's group is seeded once from napi.targets, then owned by config — never silently re-derived.
callisto matrixCI discovery
Reads napi-rs and maturin native build targets straight from manifests and emits a CI matrix as JSON — one source of truth instead of hand-maintained, drift-prone YAML arrays.
Pre-release cyclespre.json
Byte-compatible with changesets' pre.json. pre.0 → pre.1 → pre.2 stays monotonic and idempotent by computing from a snapshot of initial versions, not on-disk state.
Snapshot releasestransient
A throwaway version like 0.0.0-snapshot-<sha>, written uncommitted and untagged. Callisto never publishes it itself — that's deliberately the calling CI workflow's job.
Publish coordinator, not reimplementorregistries
Shells out to cargo publish, npm publish, twine upload — never talks to a registry HTTP API directly. Callisto's job is deciding what and when, not re-solving auth for three ecosystems.

Plate VII

Design principles

Seven rules, formally enumerated in the design doc, that every feature above answers to.

P1
Byte-compatibility is the adoption gate
Matching changesets' file format exactly is a hard requirement — nothing overrides it. A team can adopt in one commit and roll back in one commit.
P2
Statelessness for correctness
Any state file Callisto writes is gitignored and never load-bearing for a correctness decision.
P3
Idempotence per phase
Re-running a command against unchanged state produces the same result, not a compounding one.
P4
Polyglot uniformity via trait boundaries
A grammar and a workspace concept per ecosystem — not just a manifest format per ecosystem.
P5
Structural fixes over discipline
A failure class gets fixed in code — a check, an invariant, a refusal — never just documented as something to remember.
P6
Release semantics live in the core
Every wrapper — the Moon plugin, a GitHub Action — is a thin dispatcher. None of them compute bumps, cascades, publish order, or changelogs themselves.
P7
Every boundary is a versioned contract
Core-to-integration boundaries are explicit, versioned, fixtured JSON/API contracts — not an informal understanding.

Plate VIII

Command surface

Fourteen subcommands, one binary. Every one supports --format json for scripting and --dry-run where it mutates anything.

CommandWhat it does
initScaffold Callisto configuration in the current workspace.
addCreate a new changeset describing pending package changes — interactive wizard or flags.
statusShow the workspace's pending changesets and diagnostics.
validateCheck that changesets and the dependency graph are well-formed.
versionConsume pending changesets and bump package versions accordingly.
pre enter / pre exitEnter or exit prerelease mode for the workspace.
snapshotApply a temporary, non-persistent version bump for a snapshot release.
matrixPrint the workspace's native-build target matrix as JSON or a table.
plan-publishCompute which packages are ready to publish and print the plan.
publishPublish ready packages to their registries via native CLI tools.
tagCreate git tags for packages in a publish plan.
compose-pr-bodyGenerate a pull request body summarizing pending release changes.
schemaPrint the JSON schema for a report type.
completionsGenerate shell completion scripts.

Plate IX

Scale & rigor

Pre-1.0, and explicit about it — the versioned contract is --format json on stdout, not the Rust API.

**Callisto Atlas** is live: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/da690251-1a53-467a-a3a7-7641fb66ed7d

Nine plates, built entirely from real docs/source (not marketing copy):

1. **The coordination gap** — the napi wedge (1 Rust crate → N platform npm packages), quoted directly from the design doc
2. **Prior art & positioning** — named differentiation against changesets, release-please, Nx Release, and knope, plus the honest "this is a niche, not a mass-market claim" quote
3. **Origin of the name** — the crater metaphor (impacts layered in order = versions layered in history)
4. **Layered architecture** — a mermaid diagram of all 10 crates across 4 layers, colored by license (permissive vs AGPL)
5. **How a release moves** — changeset → graph → cascade → apply → tag/publish pipeline diagram
6. **Feature specimens** — 8 cards: CST-preserving edits, atomic writes, cascade engine, version groups, `callisto matrix`, pre-release cycles, snapshots, publish-coordinator posture
7. **Design principles** — the 7 P's from the design doc, condensed
8. **Command surface** — all 14 CLI subcommands
9. **Scale & rigor** — line counts per crate, test/fuzz/CI invariants, and an honest caveats box (unimplemented Java/.NET matrix targets, pre-1.0 API, the `callisto-vcs` license doc inconsistency)

Two mermaid diagrams for the architecture and pipeline — should drop straight into slides. One thing worth flagging: the research surfaced a real doc inconsistency (README/CONTRIBUTING.md call `callisto-vcs` AGPL, but its actual `Cargo.toml` says MIT/Apache-2.0) — I noted it honestly in the caveats box rather than picking one silently; it's a good candidate to fold into task #29 (ARCHITECTURE.md fixes) when we get there.

Backlog status: 18/31 shipped through task #18 (`TagIndex` tag-set reuse), all independently reviewed and committed. Ready to continue with #19 (dependency hygiene) whenever you want me to.

# Autonomous loop check

You're being invoked on a timer while the user is away or occupied. The point is to keep work moving forward without the user driving every step — finishing things they started, maintaining PRs they're building, catching problems before they come back to find them. You're a steward, not an initiator. The user set you loose on their work, and the value you provide comes from reliably advancing things they've already set in motion, not from finding new things to do.

The key tension to navigate: the user trusts you enough to run autonomously, but that trust is easily lost. Acting on what the conversation already established is safe and valuable. Inventing new work or making irreversible changes without clear authorization erodes trust fast. When you're unsure whether something falls into "continuing established work" or "inventing new work," lean toward the former only when the transcript provides clear evidence the user wanted it done. If you find yourself reaching for justifications about why a push is probably fine, that's a signal to wait.

## What to act on

The current conversation is your highest-signal source — re-read the transcript above, since everything there is something the user was actively engaged with. The strongest signal is an in-progress PR you've been building together: review comments to address and resolve, failing CI checks to diagnose (and re-enqueue if they're flakes), merge conflicts to fix. The goal is to get the PR into a state where it's ready to merge pending only human review — the user shouldn't come back to find a PR blocked on things you could have handled. After that, look for unfinished implementation where the last exchange left something half-done, and explicit "I'll also..." or "next I'll..." commitments the conversation made and didn't honor. Weaker but still real: dangling questions you could now answer, verification steps that were skipped, edge cases that were mentioned but not handled, and natural continuations that don't require new decisions.

If you find anything in this category, act on it — actually do the work, don't describe what could be done. Run the tests, don't say "you could run the tests." The whole point of autonomous operation is that work gets done while the user is away.

When the conversation transcript has nothing left, the current branch's pull/merge request on the user's SCM is the next-best place to look. This is maintenance work — valuable, but lower priority than continuing the user's active work. Find the PR/MR for the current branch via the SCM's CLI, then check three things: CI status, unresolved review threads, and whether the branch has fallen behind the base. For failing CI, pull the failing job's logs and diagnose before acting — flaky-shaped failures (timeout, runner died, transient network) can be re-enqueued; real failures need a reproduction and a minimal fix. For unresolved review threads, fetch the comment, address the feedback, push, and resolve the thread via, for example, the GitHub GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation (or the equivalent for whichever SCM the project uses). Before pushing anything, check whether someone else has pushed to the branch while you were working — if so, rebase (don't merge) to keep history clean.

When CI is green, threads are clear, and there's idle time, sweeping the branch for issues is a good use of that time — bug-hunt or simplification passes catch problems before reviewers do, saving everyone a round-trip.

If everything is genuinely quiet — no conversation work, no PR maintenance — say so in one sentence and stop. No summary of what you checked, no list of what you might do later. The user will see your message in the transcript when they come back; three consecutive "nothing to do" results means you should scale back to a quick CI check and stop, not narrate.

## Repeated invocations

If you see earlier autonomous checks in this conversation, adjust your scope accordingly. If a previous check left a question the user hasn't answered, the cost of acting depends on reversibility: for reversible actions (local edits, running tests), make your best call and proceed; for irreversible ones (pushing, deleting, sending), keep waiting — the cost of acting wrongly on something irreversible is much higher than the cost of waiting one more cycle. If three or more consecutive checks have found nothing actionable, things are quiet — do one quick CI/threads check and stop in a single line. Repeated "nothing to do" messages clutter the transcript and waste the user's attention when they come back to review.

Read and analyze freely — understanding the state of things has no blast radius. Make edits and run tests when you're confident they continue established work. Commit and push only when you're clearly continuing something the user authorized, or when the work pattern makes the intent obvious — like fixing CI on a PR you've been building together.

If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`, handle the event before deciding whether to re-arm. Use PushNotification when the loop can't move further without the user, or when something landed that they'd want to act on now: newly blocked on a decision you won't make alone, third straight tick with nothing to do, you're ending the loop, or a major update arrived (CI went red, a review changes the plan). You're right, and the evidence backs it up cleanly: `callisto-cli` has zero dependency on Moon (checked its `Cargo.toml` — nothing), and the README itself already lists Moon as just one of six ways to run Callisto (Bazel, Buck2, Nix flakes, Moon WASM, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, local Git hooks) — it doesn't privilege Moon at all. The "defensible niche is Moon workspaces" framing in `docs/00-design.md` §3.2 is dated 2026-07-24 and reads like an early, cautious positioning call (avoid overclaiming against mature incumbents) that the architecture has since outgrown. The tool doesn't need to claim to be "the polyglot release tool" to be broader than what that quote says — the honest claim now looks more like "native Cargo+npm+PyPI coordination with real napi support, that also happens to plug into Moon, Bazel, and CI directly," not "a Moon plugin with cross-registry awareness."

This affects two things: the design doc's positioning section, and the Atlas artifact I just published, which quotes that exact "not the polyglot release tool... Moon workspaces" line in two places (Plates I and II).

# Library-first vs. moon-first: resolving §0.1

**Summary of the recommendation.** Take **Option C**, but with a much narrower definition of "library-first" than §0.1 currently implies. The evidence from release-please, Nx Release, semantic-release, and knope does *not* support Option B's premise — that callisto has three equally-weighted consumers — because callisto's own design has already decided the GitHub Action is a bash-composite that shells out to the CLI binary (§12.1), not an independent API consumer. That leaves exactly two real consumers: `callisto-cli` and `callisto-moon` — and the second reaches the core through a narrow, enumerated I/O seam (see "Crate-boundary implications" below) and gets no independent API-stability promise, rather than a symmetric second API surface. What the prior art actually validates is not consumer symmetry but **seam placement**: Nx's v21 rewrite was caused by ecosystem I/O logic being smeared into coordination logic, and knope's cascade is permanently trapped inside its binary crate. So: keep the coordination core moon-free and binary-free as a hard, CI-enforced rule; ship moon as the one blessed integration; and do *not* pay for a stable public Rust API, a C ABI, or dyn-compatible traits before v1.0. One concrete correction falls out of this: `MoonProjectGraphResolver` as specced in §15 is the wrong shape and should be deleted — moon's project graph structurally cannot supply the data §7.4's cascade rules need.

input.prompt:
You are independently reviewing a completed fix in the Callisto Rust workspace at /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch: main, uncommitted changes in the working tree — do NOT commit, just review).

## Context

This is backlog task #19 of a 31-item remediation backlog: "Fix workspace_relative to use camino/path-slash instead of hand-rolled parsing." `crates/callisto-model/src/path.rs`'s `workspace_relative()` function normalizes an arbitrary relative path (rejecting absolute paths and lexically resolving `.`/`..` components) into a canonical, `/`-separated, workspace-root-relative `PathBuf`.

The OLD implementation did:
1. `p.to_str().is_none()` → manual UTF-8 check
2. `p.to_str().unwrap().replace('\\', "/")` → **unconditionally** treat every backslash character as a path separator, on every platform

A workspace audit flagged step 2 as "byte-incorrect on POSIX": on POSIX/Unix, `\` is a completely legal filename character, not a separator. So a real path like `"weird\file.txt"` (a POSIX filename literally containing a backslash) would get corrupted into `"weird/file.txt"` — silently referring to a different file. The audit's prescribed fix: use `camino::Utf8PathBuf::from_path_buf()` for the UTF-8 check, and `path_slash::PathExt::to_slash()` for separator normalization — both crates were already declared as workspace dependencies (`camino = "1"`, `path-slash = "0.2"`) with zero actual usages anywhere in the codebase before this fix.

## The fix

1. `crates/callisto-model/Cargo.toml`: added `path-slash.workspace = true` (camino was already present).
2. `crates/callisto-model/src/path.rs`: replaced the manual UTF-8 check with `Utf8PathBuf::from_path_buf(p.to_path_buf()).map_err(|path| ModelError::NonUtf8Path { path })?`, and replaced `.replace('\\', "/")` with `utf8.as_std_path().to_slash()`.

**Critical semantic detail to verify yourself, don't just trust this description**: I read `path_slash` 0.2.1's actual source (`~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/path-slash-0.2.1/src/lib.rs`). `PathExt::to_slash()` is `#[cfg]`-gated: on `target_os = "windows"` it walks `Path::components()` and rewrites the native `\` separator to `/`; on every other OS it's literally `self.to_str().map(Cow::Borrowed)` — a **complete no-op pass-through that never touches backslash characters at all**. This means the fix is a genuine, deliberate BEHAVIOR CHANGE on POSIX: backslashes in path strings are no longer treated as separators there, ever — which is the whole point (fixing the corruption bug), but it's worth you confirming I've correctly understood and correctly implemented this platform-conditional semantic, not just assumed it.

input.prompt:
You are independently reviewing a completed fix in the Callisto Rust workspace at /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch: main, uncommitted changes in the working tree — do NOT commit, just review).

## Context

This is backlog task #20 of a 31-item remediation backlog: "Apply dunce::canonicalize consistently at remaining path-canonicalization sites." A workspace audit found 4 raw `std::path::Path::canonicalize()`/`std::fs::canonicalize()` call sites that should use `dunce::canonicalize` instead, matching the one place in the codebase that was already doing this correctly (`crates/callisto-vcs/src/lib.rs:200`, inside `GitRepository::discover`).

Why this matters: on Windows, `std::fs::canonicalize` returns UNC-prefixed paths (`\\?\C:\...`), which many other Windows tools/APIs choke on. `dunce::canonicalize` strips that prefix when it's safe to do so, falling back to std's behavior otherwise. On non-Windows platforms, `dunce::canonicalize` is a pure passthrough to `std::fs::canonicalize` — byte-identical behavior, confirmed by reading `dunce` 1.0.5's actual source (`~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/dunce-1.0.5/src/lib.rs`), which gates all its UNC-stripping logic behind `#[cfg(windows)]`.

## The fix

1. Added `dunce = { workspace = true }` to `crates/callisto-cli/Cargo.toml` and `crates/callisto-graph/Cargo.toml` (the workspace root `Cargo.toml` already declares `dunce = "1"`; `callisto-vcs` already had it).
2. Four call sites changed from `<path>.canonicalize()` to `dunce::canonicalize(<path>)`, preserving each site's existing error-handling shape exactly (no other logic touched):
   - `crates/callisto-cli/src/workspace.rs:13` — `global.cwd.canonicalize().map_err(...)?` → `dunce::canonicalize(&global.cwd).map_err(...)?`
   - `crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/pre.rs:124` — same pattern, same file's `PreArgs::Exit` handler
   - `crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs:24` — `root.canonicalize().unwrap_or_else(|_| root.to_path_buf())` → `dunce::canonicalize(root).unwrap_or_else(|_| root.to_path_buf())`
   - `crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/root.rs:7` — same fallback pattern, in `find_workspace_root`

## What's already verified by the implementer (me) before you look

- Because `dunce::canonicalize` is byte-identical to `std::fs::canonicalize` on this platform (macOS), there is NO way to write a test on this machine that observably distinguishes old vs. new behavior — the fix is exclusively a Windows-correctness improvement. I could not do a mutation-test-by-hand verification the way I did for tasks #18/#19, since there's nothing to mutate that would produce a different observable result here. I'm flagging this explicitly rather than pretending a red/green cycle happened when it structurally couldn't on this platform.
- To compensate, I ran `cargo check -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` rustup target was already installed in this environment from a prior task's review). It completed with exit code 0 after ~6.5 minutes, type-checking both crates' `#[cfg(windows)]`-gated `dunce::canonicalize` code path for real, which I could not do by reading source alone.
- `cargo build --workspace` — clean
- `cargo test -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph` (full suite, both crates) — all pass, including `locate::ignore_walk`'s 3 tests specifically
- `cargo clippy -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph` — applied, no changes needed beyond formatting already in place

Do NOT re-run the full test suite/clippy/fmt yourself unless you have specific reason to doubt something — trust that baseline. DO feel free to re-run the Windows cross-compile check yourself if you want independent confirmation rather than trusting my report of it, and spot-check anything suspicious by reading code.

## What to review

1. **Read the actual current diff** (`git diff crates/callisto-cli/src/workspace.rs crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/pre.rs crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/root.rs crates/callisto-cli/Cargo.toml crates/callisto-graph/Cargo.toml`) — don't just trust this description.
2. **Confirm the substitution preserves error semantics exactly.** `dunce::canonicalize`'s signature is `pub fn canonicalize<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> io::Result<PathBuf>` — same as `std::fs::canonicalize`/`Path::canonicalize`. Confirm each of the 4 call sites' surrounding `.map_err(...)` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)` logic is byte-for-byte unchanged except for the swapped function call, and that no borrow-checker-driven change (e.g. needing `&global.cwd` instead of the original method-call receiver syntax) silently altered anything else.
3. **Sibling gaps — this is the important one.** Search the ENTIRE workspace (not just the 4 files already touched) for any other raw `.canonicalize()` call, including in `callisto-moon`, test helper code, fixtures, build scripts, or anywhere else — including patterns that might not literally read `.canonicalize()` but achieve the same effect (e.g. `std::fs::canonicalize(...)` called as a free function rather than a method, or a re-export). The original audit that spawned this task claimed exactly 4 remaining sites plus the 1 already-correct `callisto-vcs` site — verify that count is actually accurate against the current codebase, not stale.
4. **Confirm `dunce` is actually a permissively-licensed crate** (MIT or similar) — this task touches `callisto-cli` and `callisto-graph`, both AGPL-3.0-only crates per CLAUDE.md's layering, so license compatibility isn't a structural concern here, but worth a fast sanity check since a new dependency was added to two crates.
5. **Check whether the two crates' `Cargo.toml` additions are placed sensibly** relative to their existing dependency list ordering/conventions (some crates in this workspace seem to keep dependencies loosely alphabetized within sections) — purely cosmetic, not a correctness issue, just note if it's inconsistent with the surrounding file's own convention.

Report back concisely: a list of concrete findings (file:line, what's wrong, why it matters), separating "must fix before commit" from "worth noting but not blocking." If you find nothing wrong, say so plainly — don't manufacture findings. Keep your report under 500 words plus the findings list.

input.prompt:
You are independently reviewing a completed batch of changes in the Callisto Rust workspace at /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch: main, uncommitted changes in the working tree — do NOT commit, just review).

## Context

This is a batched commit covering backlog tasks #21, #22, and #23 of a 35-item remediation backlog — the approved plan explicitly proposed grouping these three specifically because none involve meaningful new test coverage the way earlier tasks did (they're mechanical dependency-hygiene / Cargo.toml changes), verified via build+test+tree rather than a strict red/green TDD cycle per item. Task #23 is the exception — it got real new test coverage, described below.

## The three changes

**Task #21 — Move `tempfile` to dev-dependencies in `callisto-changelog`.**
`crates/callisto-changelog/Cargo.toml` had `tempfile = { workspace = true }` under `[dependencies]` (production), but grep confirmed all actual usages are inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in `crates/callisto-changelog/src/write.rs` (5 call sites, all `tempfile::tempdir()`), never in production code. Moved the declaration to `[dev-dependencies]`. Verified via `cargo tree -p callisto-changelog -e normal` still showing `tempfile` (because `callisto-model`, a dependency of `callisto-changelog`, ALSO directly depends on `tempfile` in its own `[dependencies]` — separate, out-of-scope pre-existing declaration) — so I additionally ran `cargo tree -i tempfile -e normal` (inverse tree) to confirm `callisto-changelog` no longer has a DIRECT edge to `tempfile` in the production graph, only a transitive one via `callisto-model`.

**Task #22 — Remove unused `serde_yaml` dependency and dead `ConfigError::ParseYaml` variant.**
`crates/callisto-graph/Cargo.toml` declared `serde_yaml = { workspace = true }` with zero actual `serde_yaml::` usages anywhere in `crates/callisto-graph/src/` (confirmed via grep before touching anything). The only YAML-related file handling in that crate is `crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/root.rs:46`, which does `dir.join("pnpm-workspace.yaml").exists()` — an existence check only, never actually parses YAML content. `ConfigError::ParseYaml { path: PathBuf, message: String }` (diagnostic code E112) in `crates/callisto-graph/src/error.rs` was likewise never constructed anywhere (confirmed via grep across the whole workspace, only its own definition site matched) — `ConfigError` is `#[non_exhaustive]` so removing the variant doesn't force any exhaustive-match updates. Removed both the Cargo.toml dependency line and the enum variant. Also removed the now-fully-unused `serde_yaml = "0.9"` line from the workspace root `Cargo.toml`'s `[workspace.dependencies]` section, since after this change no crate in the workspace declares it anymore (confirmed via grep across all `crates/*/Cargo.toml`). Note: `serde_yaml` still appears in `Cargo.lock`/`cargo tree` output as a transitive dependency of `wasmtime`/`wasm-compose` via `callisto-moon`'s test-utils chain — that's unrelated to this fix, a third-party crate's own internal dependency, not something in our control or in scope.

**Task #23 — Use the `semver` crate in `check_git_version` instead of hand-rolled parsing.**
`crates/callisto-model/src/exec.rs`'s `check_git_version(reported: &str)` used to hand-parse a `git --version`-style string by splitting on `.` and doing `major < 2 || (major == 2 && minor < 20)` — a numeric comparison hardcoded separately from the `REQUIRED_GIT: &str = ">=2.20"` constant used only for the error message, meaning the two could silently drift out of sync if either was changed without the other. Rewrote to: extract the leading whitespace-delimited digit-starting word, take at most its first 3 dot-separated components (defaulting missing minor/patch to `"0"`, and discarding anything beyond the 3rd component — needed because Git for Windows reports versions like `"2.39.5.windows.1"`, which has a non-semver `.windows.N` suffix that would otherwise fail `semver::Version::parse`), parse that as `semver::Version`, parse `REQUIRED_GIT` as `semver::VersionReq`, and use `VersionReq::matches()` for the actual comparison — making the floor defined in exactly one place. Added 4 new tests (`rejects_versions_just_below_the_required_floor`, `ignores_trailing_windows_suffix`, `treats_missing_patch_as_zero`, `rejects_unparseable_version_string`) alongside the pre-existing `parses_git_version`.

## What's already verified by the implementer (me) before you look

- I mutation-tested task #23's fix by hand: temporarily inverted the `if required.matches(&version) { Ok(()) } else { Err(...) }` branch to `if !required.matches(&version)`, reran the 5 `exec::tests::*` tests, confirmed 4 of 5 failed with the expected assertion messages (the 5th, `rejects_unparseable_version_string`, correctly still passed since garbage input fails to parse before ever reaching the `matches()` call, unaffected by the inversion) — then restored the real fix and confirmed byte-identical restoration via `diff`.
- Note `check_git_version` currently has ZERO callers anywhere in the workspace outside its own test module (confirmed via grep) — it's dead/unwired production code, a pre-existing gap from an earlier audit ("built and exported but never called anywhere and never tested; wire it in or remove it") that is explicitly NOT part of this task's scope (this task only fixes the parsing/comparison logic itself, doesn't wire it in).
- `cargo build --workspace` — clean, zero errors
- `cargo test --workspace` — full suite, all green, zero failures (confirmed via grep for "FAILED" excluding "0 failed" false-positive matches)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean (this DID catch a real lint mid-development: `clippy::map_err_ignore` on two `.map_err(|_| ...)` calls in the new `check_git_version`, fixed by naming the ignored bindings `_parse_err` instead of `_`)
- `cargo fmt -p callisto-model -p callisto-graph -p callisto-changelog` — applied

Do NOT re-run the full test suite/clippy/fmt yourself unless you have specific reason to doubt something — trust that baseline, but DO spot-check by reading code and running narrowly-scoped commands (e.g. `cargo test -p callisto-model --lib exec::`, `cargo tree` variants) if something looks off.

## What to review

1. **Read the actual current diff** for all touched files: `git diff Cargo.toml crates/callisto-changelog/Cargo.toml crates/callisto-graph/Cargo.toml crates/callisto-graph/src/error.rs crates/callisto-model/src/exec.rs` — don't just trust this description.
2. **Task #21**: confirm the `cargo tree` reasoning is actually correct — run `cargo tree -i tempfile -e normal` yourself and confirm `callisto-changelog` really has no direct edge, only a transitive one via `callisto-model`.
3. **Task #22**: confirm `ConfigError::ParseYaml` and `serde_yaml` really are unreferenced workspace-wide (not just in the files I checked) — do your own grep sweep, including `.rs` files I might not have thought to check (test files, fixtures, doc-comments referencing the diagnostic code E112 by name that might now be stale/dangling). Also check whether `docs/01-spec.md` or `ARCHITECTURE.md` mention `E112`/`ParseYaml`/YAML parsing as if it were real, which would now be stale documentation (not something to fix in this task, but worth flagging like previous review findings that spawned follow-up tasks #34/#35).
4. **Task #23 — this is the one with real logic to scrutinize.** Trace through the parsing logic yourself for edge cases I may not have considered: what does `check_git_version("git version 2.39.5-rc1")` do (a real pre-release suffix, which semver DOES support via hyphen — does my `splitn(4, '.').take(3)` truncation logic handle `"5-rc1"` as the third `.`-split component correctly when parsed as part of `core`, i.e. does `semver::Version::parse("2.39.5-rc1")` succeed, and if so is treating a pre-release git build as satisfying `>=2.20` semantically correct or does semver's pre-release comparison rules cause a false rejection)? What about a 4-component CalVer-style version some tools report (e.g. `"2.39.0.1"` without any Windows-suffix marker)? Does the truncation-to-3-components silently accept an ambiguous/wrong interpretation there? Is there any version string shape where the OLD hand-rolled logic and the NEW semver-based logic would disagree on accept/reject, beyond the ones I already tested?
5. **Test quality for task #23's new tests**: read them directly, confirm they test what they claim, and confirm my mutation-testing claim (4-of-5 failing under the inverted-logic mutation) is itself accurate by re-deriving why `rejects_unparseable_version_string` would legitimately be unaffected by that specific mutation.
6. **Sibling gaps**: any other hand-rolled version-comparison logic elsewhere in the workspace (search broadly — `major.*minor`, manual `.split('.')` version parsing, etc.) that has the same "drift from a separately-declared requirement string" risk this task fixed, and wasn't touched?

Report back concisely: a list of concrete findings (file:line, what's wrong, why it matters), separating "must fix before commit" from "worth noting but not blocking." If you find nothing wrong, say so plainly — don't manufacture findings. Keep your report under 600 words plus the findings list.

  >=2.20 floor is defined in exactly one place (REQUIRED_GIT) instead

  drift from it. Handles Git for Windows's non-semver ".windows.N"
  suffix by truncating to the first three dot-separated components,

  build tag (e.g. "2.39.5-rc1") doesn't fall afoul of semver's
  pre-release exclusion rules and get falsely rejected — caught by
  independent review, verified by hand-reverting the strip and
  confirming the new test fails for the right reason.

Also fixes a stale "E112" entry in callisto-model's
test_all_diagnostic_codes_are_unique list, left dangling by the

   - `petgraph`: `callisto-graph` only (the only crate that uses it at all; was `"0.6"`, workspace already declares `petgraph = "0.6"`)

**`matrix` (§M.12.8, §CLI.6.13).** Read-only and on-demand: unlike the four functions above, it
does not participate in the release cycle, consumes no changesets, and touches no `TagIndex`.
For each package in scope (all registered packages, or exactly one under `opts.package`, which
is `Err(GraphError::UnknownPackage)` if the name doesn't match anything — checked before any
manifest is read, so an unknown `--package` never reaches a parse), it reads at most one
`package.json` and one `pyproject.toml`, shares each parsed value between the platform-target
and runtime-version derivations for that package (§G.1's P2 — one read, not one per
consumer), and produces two independent map entries: `platformTargets[name]` from
`napi.targets`/`[tool.maturin].targets`, and `runtimeVersions[name]` from
`engines.node`/`requires-python`. A package can contribute to either map, both, or neither; the
two are computed and reported independently.

A platform-target entry's `targets[]` comes from a per-triple join of two independently-pinned
tables: `napi.rs`'s `triple_to_role` (platform/arch/abi — shared with §G.4.5's unrelated napi
platform auto-derivation, which this module does not otherwise touch) and a table of exactly 18
`(hostRunner, useCross)` pairs new to this module (§G.11's justification: `ManifestRole::Platform`
carries no CI-scheduling information, so it cannot be derived from the shared table alone).
`artifactName` is always `"native-" + triple`. A triple absent from *either* table is excluded
from `targets[]` and reported as an `UnrecognisedPlatformTriple` diagnostic naming the triple and
the package — never a hard error, since one unrecognised triple in a declaration must not hide
the ones that were recognised. A triple repeated within one package's own declaration is
likewise not an error: the duplicate is dropped (first occurrence wins) and reported as
`DuplicatePlatformTriple`, since a hand-maintained `napi.targets` array is exactly the kind of
list a copy-paste duplicates without anyone noticing, and two identical `PlatformTarget` entries
would mean two identical CI jobs racing on the same artifact upload.

A package declaring platform targets via **both** `napi.targets` and `[tool.maturin].targets` —
even as an explicitly empty array on one side — is `Err(GraphError::ConflictingPlatformTargetSources)`
(AC-017): there is no principled way to prefer one source over the other, so neither is used.
A runtime-version entry orders `engines.node` before `requires-python` when a package declares
both (AC-005b) — arbitrary as a tiebreak, but fixed so `--format json` output is deterministic
run to run.

> `[SPEC DECISION, not in 00-design.md: neither `UnrecognisedPlatformTriple` nor
> `DuplicatePlatformTriple` carries an `escalated_by`, and `matrix`'s command handler never
> calls §G.11's `escalate`.]` Every other command function's diagnostics are subject to
> `--strict`/`--strict-graph` promotion (§G.11's opening paragraph); `matrix` has neither flag
> on `MatrixOptions` at all. `matrix` is a read-only discovery report consumed by CI tooling
> that expects a matrix even when some packages have manifest quirks — a workspace with one
> unrecognised triple should still emit a usable matrix for every other package, not fail the
> whole CI run on the strength of an unregistered target platform. Malformed manifest *syntax*
> (§AC-010/010b/010c) is still a hard `Err`, since there is no report to degrade to once a
> `package.json`/`pyproject.toml` doesn't parse at all — the diagnostic path exists specifically
> for the "each half parsed fine, this platform triple is merely unrecognised" case.

     pub fn check_git_version(reported: &str) -> Result<(), CommandError> {
         let incompatible = || CommandError::IncompatibleVersion {
             program: "git".to_string(),
             found: reported.to_string(),
             required: REQUIRED_GIT.to_string(),
         };
         let version_str = reported.trim();
         let digits = version_str
             .split_whitespace()
             .find(|word| word.chars().next().is_some_and(|c| c.is_ascii_digit()))
             .unwrap_or(version_str);
         let mut parts = digits.splitn(4, '.').take(3);
         let major = leading_digits(parts.next().unwrap_or("0"));
         let minor = leading_digits(parts.next().unwrap_or("0"));
         let patch = leading_digits(parts.next().unwrap_or("0"));
         let core = format!("{major}.{minor}.{patch}");
         let version = semver::Version::parse(&core).map_err(|_parse_err| incompatible())?;
         let required = semver::VersionReq::parse(REQUIRED_GIT).map_err(|_parse_err| incompatible())?;
         if required.matches(&version) { Ok(()) } else { Err(incompatible()) }

809	## 9. Publish planning
810	
811	**This section is the biggest change from the prior revision.** Callisto is a
812	**versioning coordinator**, not a release orchestrator. It decides what should happen and
813	updates the workspace to reflect the decision; it does not run the actual publish. The
814	underlying ecosystem tools (`cargo`, `npm`/`pnpm`, and whatever future ecosystem tool)
815	already do registry auth, retries, rate-limit handling, and idempotence — reimplementing
816	any of that inside callisto would be redundant and would put callisto in the business of
817	tracking every registry's quirks, which is not where its value is.
818	
819	### 9.1 What callisto produces
820	
821	Three outputs, all read-only with respect to any registry:
822	
823	1. **On-disk state** — the result of `callisto version`: updated manifests, deleted
824	   consumed changesets, regenerated changelogs, optionally refreshed lockfiles.
825	2. **A publish plan** (`callisto plan-publish --format json`) — describes what needs
826	   publishing, to what registry, in what order, without executing anything.
827	3. **Git tags** — **never created at `version` time.** `version` only computes and writes
828	   manifests; it does not touch tags at all. Tag *names* are computed by callisto (one
829	   function, below) and appear in the plan's `releases[].tagName` (§9.2), but the tags
830	   themselves are only ever created by explicitly invoking `callisto tag` (or the workflow's
831	   own `git tag` using the plan's `tagName`/`sha` fields, per §9.3's example) **after the
832	   corresponding publish has actually succeeded** — never preemptively. This is the resolved
833	   answer to what was previously three disagreeing accounts of tag ownership: a tag's mere
834	   existence is P2's stateless signal that a release happened, so creating one before the
835	   publish it represents has actually succeeded would let a partial failure masquerade as a
836	   completed release on the next run — precisely the failure mode P2 exists to prevent, not
837	   cause. Pushing stays a separate, later step, always done by the calling workflow, never
838	   by callisto (§13 invariant 16's push-last rule) — `callisto tag` creates local tags only.
839	
840	   **Tag name resolution is one function, used identically everywhere a tag name is
841	   needed** (§7.5's group-forcing, `releases[].tagName`, and `last_tag_for`'s search) — this
842	   is the concrete fix for the failure release-please's `#2207` documents (two independently-
843	   evolved identity/tag-resolution code paths silently disagreeing). `PackageId` +
844	   `tag_template` (§5.1) → tag string lives in `callisto-model`. **Grammar**: `tag_template`
845	   supports exactly one placeholder, `{version}`; there is no `{name}` placeholder, because
846	   the package name is already fixed per-`Package` (it's not something a template needs to
847	   interpolate — a template is scoped to one package by construction). The **default**, when
848	   `tag_template` is unset, is `{name}@{version}` with `{name}` substituted once from the
849	   `Package`'s bare or shortest-unambiguous identity form (§5.4) — this is where §12.6's
850	   `<name>@<version>` convention comes from; it's the default template's literal shape, not a
851	   second placeholder grammar. Because an arbitrary `{version}`-interpolated template is not
852	   generally invertible, `last_tag_for` never parses tag strings against the template — it
853	   validates at config-load time that a `tag_template` contains `{version}` exactly once,
854	   derives a literal glob from everything else in the template (`foo@{version}` → match
855	   `foo@*`), lists matching tags via that glob, and picks the highest by parsing only the
856	   substring at the placeholder's position as a SemVer (or per-ecosystem, §7.7) version —
857	   never by attempting to invert the template as a whole.
858	
859	### 9.2 The plan's shape
860	
861	```json
862	{
863	  "schemaVersion": 1,
864	  "rustCrates": [
865	    { "name": "foo", "version": "1.3.0", "publishTo": "cratesIo" }
866	  ],
867	  "npmPlatformPackages": [
868	    { "name": "@myorg/foo-linux-x64-gnu", "version": "1.3.0", "publishTo": "npm" }
869	  ],
870	  "npmMainPackages": [
871	    { "name": "@myorg/foo", "version": "1.3.0", "publishTo": "npm",
872	      "dependsOnPlatforms": ["@myorg/foo-linux-x64-gnu", "..."] }
873	  ],
874	  "releases": [
875	    { "tagName": "foo@1.3.0", "sha": "...", "changelogSection": "..." }
876	  ]
877	}
878	```
879	
880	The **ordering implied by the plan's structure** (Rust crates → platform npm packages →
881	main npm packages) is the correctness-relevant fact callisto is responsible for — napi main
882	packages reference their platforms via `optionalDependencies` at exact versions, so those
883	must exist on the registry first, or installs `404`. Getting this ordering right is
884	callisto's job; *executing* the publishes in that order is the calling workflow's job.
885	`rustCrates[]`'s array order **is** the intra-release topological order (§13 invariant 7) —
886	load-bearing, not incidental, and part of the fixtured contract (§12.5/§12.6).
887	
888	`releases[].sha` is **HEAD at `plan-publish` invocation time** — callisto never commits
889	(§7.6 step 11), so this is necessarily after the calling workflow's own commit of
890	`version`'s output (§9.3's example runs `git commit` before `plan-publish`), never before.
891	A workflow that reorders those two steps gets a `sha` for the pre-bump commit, which is a
892	misuse of the contract, not an ambiguity in it.
893	
894	`releases[]` contains one entry per **tag-bearing** package only — the napi main package and
895	(if separately published) the crate. Platform packages appear in `npmPlatformPackages[]` for
896	publishing but never in `releases[]`: they are never independently tagged (§7.5), since they
897	are dependents-in-lockstep with the main package's release, not separate release points.
898	
899	### 9.3 What this looks like in practice
900	
901	```bash
902	callisto version
903	git commit -am "chore: version packages"
904	
905	callisto plan-publish --format json > plan.json
906	
907	# Rust: topo-sorted from the plan
908	jq -r '.rustCrates[].name' plan.json | while read c; do cargo publish -p "$c"; done
909	
910	# npm: platforms first, mains second — the plan's structure already encodes this order
911	pnpm -r publish --filter "$(jq -r '.npmPlatformPackages[].name' plan.json | paste -sd, -)"
912	pnpm -r publish --filter "$(jq -r '.npmMainPackages[].name' plan.json | paste -sd, -)"
913	
914	# Tag on success — this is what closes the stateless-detection loop for next time
915	jq -r '.releases[] | "\(.tagName) \(.sha)"' plan.json | while read tag sha; do
916	  git tag "$tag" "$sha"
917	done
918	git push --tags
919	```
920	
921	The tag creation on success is the signal that makes next run's stateless detection work —
922	no callisto command "reads back" what got published; the tag existing (or not) at the
923	expected version is the only source of truth.
924	
925	### 9.4 Idempotence — two layers
926	
927	**Publish idempotence** is provided by the ecosystem tools: `cargo publish` refuses to
928	overwrite an existing version; so does `npm publish`. Callisto relies on this for publish
929	retry safety rather than re-implementing "is this already published?" registry queries. If a
930	`plan-publish` output names a package that's already on the registry, the ecosystem tool's
931	own refusal is the safety net — cheap, correct, and not callisto's problem to duplicate.
932	
933	**Version-apply idempotence** is provided by callisto itself: `apply_version_plan` reads each
934	manifest's current on-disk version before writing. If it matches `bump.to` (the target version
935	was already written by a prior crashed run), the write is skipped and the path is staged
936	without modification — safe to retry. If it matches neither `bump.from` nor `bump.to`, the
937	function returns `Err(GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion)` to require human intervention
938	rather than silently writing an unplanned version. Changeset paths are always staged regardless
939	of whether the changeset file exists on disk, so `git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch` cleans
940	the index on retry even after a prior run deleted the file.
941	
942	### 9.5 What this removes from the prior design
943	
944	The prior revision specified a 7-phase *orchestration* pipeline that callisto itself would
945	execute: `cargo publish -p <name> --registry <key>` calls with retry-with-backoff on
946	rate-limit errors, registry-API idempotence queries (`GET /api/v1/crates/...`, `npm view
947	...`), an `on-failure: aggregate | abort` policy, and octocrab/reqwest/tokio in the CLI's
948	core dependency tree for GitHub release creation. All of that is removed. It was solving a
949	problem — coordinating a polyglot publish sequence — that's better solved by computing the
950	right plan and letting each ecosystem's own, more mature tool execute its slice.
951	
952	This significantly shrinks the CLI's dependency surface and the amount of registry-specific
953	logic that needs testing.
954

## 19. `callisto matrix`

**Read-only CI matrix generation, not a planning or publish command.** Once a workspace
has `napi`- or `maturin`-based platform packages (§7.5), the calling CI workflow needs to
know which OS/arch/ABI triples to build on, which GitHub-Actions-style runner label and
`use-cross` setting each triple needs, and which Node/Python engine ranges each package
declares — all before it can construct its own build matrix. `callisto matrix` answers
exactly that question by reading each package's manifest (`napi.targets` or
`[tool.maturin].targets`, plus `engines.node`/`requires-python`) and reporting the union,
without computing a version plan, touching any file, or talking to a registry.

Deliberately absent: no `--dry-run` flag (the command has no side effect to suppress), no
interaction with the cascade or publish plan (a triple appearing here says nothing about
whether the package it belongs to is ready to release), and no attempt to *validate* the
CI configuration a caller builds from this data (the calling workflow owns whatever
`strategy.matrix` shape it constructs from the JSON).

### 19.1 What it reports

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "platformTargets": {
    "@myorg/foo": {
      "kind": "napi",
      "source": "napi.targets",
      "targets": [
        {
          "triple": "aarch64-apple-darwin",
          "platform": "darwin",
          "arch": "arm64",
          "abi": null,
          "hostRunner": "macos-latest",
          "useCross": false,
          "artifactName": "native-aarch64-apple-darwin",
          "packageDir": "packages/foo",
          "packageName": "@myorg/foo"
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "runtimeVersions": {
    "@myorg/foo": [
      { "ecosystem": "npm", "field": "engines.node", "range": ">=18" }
    ]
  }
}
```

Both top-level maps are keyed by the *registered package's* `PackageId::name()` — not by
triple or by manifest path — so a caller resolving CI jobs per package (the common case:
one build job fans out over that package's own triples) never has to invert an
index. Map ordering is lexicographic by construction (`BTreeMap`), so output is stable
across runs without a separate sort step. `platformTargets[pkg].targets` is itself sorted
ascending by triple string for the same reason.

A package with no `napi.targets`/`[tool.maturin].targets` and no
`engines.node`/`requires-python` simply has no entry in either map — matrix never
synthesizes a placeholder, and an empty workspace produces
`{"schemaVersion":1,"platformTargets":{},"runtimeVersions":{}}` with no `diagnostics` key
at all (an empty array is never serialized, matching every other report type's convention
of omitting rather than emitting an empty `diagnostics: []`).

### 19.2 The host-runner table is new data, not derived data

`napi::triple_to_role` (§7.5) already recognizes each of the (currently 18) supported
triples well enough to classify them into `ManifestRole::Platform` — but that
classification carries only platform/arch/abi, because that's all `napi.targets` drift
checking ever needed. Which GitHub Actions runner label builds a given triple, and
whether it needs `cross` rather than native `cargo build`, is CI-scheduling knowledge with
no other consumer in callisto — so `matrix` owns a second, independent
triple-to-scheduling-hint table rather than trying to widen `triple_to_role`'s existing
contract to serve a second, unrelated purpose. A triple `triple_to_role` doesn't recognize
is reported via a diagnostic (§19.3), never silently defaulted to some runner guess.

### 19.3 Diagnostics, not errors

Matches §13's general escalation posture (invariant 22): everything `matrix` finds wrong
is reported as data in the response, never as a process failure that aborts CI before a
human sees what's actually broken. An unrecognized platform triple
(`UnrecognisedPlatformTriple`) or two manifest sources both claiming platform-target
ownership for one package (`ConflictingPlatformTargetSources`, surfaced as
`GraphError::ConflictingPlatformTargetSources` — the one case that *is* a hard `Err`,
because there is no well-defined single group to report if napi and maturin config
disagree about what this package's targets even are) both produce diagnostics rather than
non-zero exit codes on their own; `--strict` (shared with every other command, §13
invariant 22) is what promotes them to a failing exit code, and that choice belongs to the
calling workflow, not to `matrix` itself.

### 19.4 Where it sits relative to publish planning

`matrix` and `plan-publish` (§9) read overlapping manifest fields but answer different
questions on different schedules: `plan-publish` runs once, after `version`, to decide
*what* ships this release; `matrix` runs independently, typically once per CI trigger
before any version decision exists yet, to decide *which machines* need to exist to build
whatever eventually ships. A workspace with no pending changesets still has a matrix (the
triples don't change just because nothing is releasing this run) — this is why `matrix`
takes no changeset/cascade input at all and cannot be affected by cascade or pre-mode
state (§7, §8).

10838	2. **Cycle Diagnostics**: When graph traversal encounters a circular dependency, the solver MUST run Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components algorithm (`petgraph::algo::tarjan_scc`) to isolate the cyclic nodes and construct a `Diagnostic` with code `callisto::circular_dependency` detailing the exact cycle path (`pkg-a → pkg-b → pkg-a`).

10841	1. **Schema Derivation**: All serializable configuration and state types in `callisto-model` (`CallistoConfig`, `PreState`, `Changeset`, `Severity`, `Version`) MUST derive `schemars::JsonSchema`.
